seoDescription: Learn the fundamentals of creating Django models for a web application by building a blueprint for a music library. This tutorial explains how to define your data structure in Python, creating `Album` and `Song` models with fields like `CharField`. Discover how Django models automatically map to your database schema, simplifying backend development.

chapters.title: What are Django Models?
chapters.description: This chapter introduces the concept of Django models as blueprints that define both the Python objects and the database schema for your application.

chapters.title: Creating the Album Model
chapters.description: Learn how to create your first model by defining an `Album` class with various `CharField` attributes for the artist, title, genre, and logo.

chapters.title: Linking Songs to Albums with Foreign Keys
chapters.description: This chapter demonstrates how to create a `Song` model and link it to the `Album` model using a `ForeignKey`, establishing a many-to-one relationship.

chapters.title: Primary Keys vs. Foreign Keys
chapters.description: An explanation of the difference between primary keys, which uniquely identify an object, and foreign keys, which link one object to another.

chapters.title: The `on_delete=CASCADE` Behavior
chapters.description: Discover the purpose of `on_delete=models.CASCADE` and how it automatically manages the deletion of related objects in your database.

chapters.title: Finalizing the Song Model
chapters.description: This chapter completes the `Song` model by adding the final `file_type` and `song_title` fields, finishing the data blueprints for the music app.

summary:
## Django Models: The Blueprint for Your Data

In Django, a **model** is a Python class that defines the blueprint for your application's data. It serves a dual purpose:

1.  **For Python**: It's a class you can use to create and manipulate objects (e.g., an `Album` object).
2.  **For the Database**: Django uses the model definition to automatically create a corresponding database table with columns that match your class variables.

This system means you only have to define your data structure once, right in your Python code.

## Creating the `Album` Model

To create a model, you define a class in `models.py` that inherits from `models.Model`. Each variable, or **field**, in the class represents a column in the database table.

```python
from django.db import models

class Album(models.Model):
    artist = models.CharField(max_length=250)
    album_title = models.CharField(max_length=500)
    genre = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    album_logo = models.CharField(max_length=1000)
```

-   **`CharField`** is used for text-based data.
-   **`max_length`** is a required argument for `CharField` that specifies the maximum number of characters the field can store.

## Creating the `Song` Model & Establishing Relationships

Models can be related to each other. In this example, a `Song` must belong to an `Album`.

> [!TIP]
> This is a **many-to-one** relationship: one Album can have many Songs, but each Song belongs to only one Album.

```python
class Song(models.Model):
    album = models.ForeignKey(Album, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    file_type = models.CharField(max_length=10)
    song_title = models.CharField(max_length=250)
```

## Key Concepts: Primary vs. Foreign Keys

-   **Primary Key**: A unique identifier for each object (or row) in a database table. Django automatically creates an `id` field for every model to serve as its primary key. This ensures you can always uniquely reference a specific album or song, even if other data (like titles) are duplicated.

-   **Foreign Key**: A field that links one model to another. The `album` field in the `Song` model is a `ForeignKey`. It stores the **primary key** (the `id`) of the `Album` that the song belongs to. This is how the relationship is maintained in the database.

## Understanding `on_delete=models.CASCADE`

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The `on_delete` option tells Django what to do when the object that a `ForeignKey` points to is deleted.

**`on_delete=models.CASCADE`** means that if you delete an `Album`, Django will automatically delete all the `Song` objects that were linked to it. This prevents having " orphaned" songs in your database that don't belong to any album.
